Traditional · The Seoul Table

Kimchi Jjigae

A deeply comforting stew that gives mature kimchi its next chapter.

Korean · Easy · Serves 3–4 (one pot)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: traditional — the elder jar's destiny. Kimchi jjigae is the pot the kimchi jar (#2) was always becoming: sour, elder-stage kimchi stewed with pork and tofu and a paste-and-gochugaru broth until the whole pot tastes of the ferment's second life. The rule is absolute and the record's first sentence: sour, old kimchi or no kimchi jjigae at all — the young jar's crunch reads as cabbage soup, the elder's sour reads as the dish. Heat dial: 3, and the aged kimchi brings its own.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The jar audit: two weeks-plus sour is the floor; a month is the sweet spot. If the jar runs young and the pot must happen tonight, the fix is a spoon of rice vinegar and an extra spoon of the jar's brine at the broth stage — a patch, labeled as one, that gets you half the elder's sour.
  • Everything cut before the pot — the stew builds in one motion.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The pork rendered in the dry pot first — 3–4 minutes, its fat becoming the pot's cooking base (the tuna path: the oil and the drained fish, 2 minutes). The kimchi in over the rendered pork and fried 2 minutes in the fat — this brief fry drives the kimchi's raw sour edge off and deepens the whole pot before any liquid joins. Checkpoint — the kimchi's edges go translucent and the pot's smell shifts from sharp-sour to round-sour-savory — the fry's whole achievement, worth the two minutes it costs.
  2. 02
    The stock, the dissolved gochujang, the gochugaru, and the soy in; the onion too. A steady bubble, 10 minutes, lid ajar — the broth turns the kimchi's red-orange and the pork's fat beads at the surface. Checkpoint — a spoon of broth at the 10-minute mark: sour first, then deep chile warmth, then the pork's richness — the three-part register that defines the dish. Flat sour? The jar ran young (see the audit). One-note hot? The gochugaru ran past its six grams.
  3. 03
    The tofu slabs laid in gently, 5 more minutes — warmed through, not boiled apart. The scallions, chili, garlic, and sesame oil over the top, and the pot goes to the table in its own vessel, still bubbling. Checkpoint — the eating test with rice: kimchi and broth over the rice bowl, a slab of tofu beside, and the pot's sour-heat should open the appetite rather than close it — the jjigae's entire purpose. The noodle or rice drop at the pot's final act (the last five minutes of broth, never longer) is the table's shared last course, and the fight over it is the meal's traditional ending. Chef’s Note — the elder-jar economy is the dish's whole logic: every kimchi batch rides an arc from fresh-crunchy to sour-complex, and the tradition built this pot as the arc's purpose — the stage that would be "getting old" in a Western fridge is, in this kitchen, the stage the stew pot was waiting for. One jar, two dishes, zero waste: the young jar's banchan bowl and the elder jar's stew pot are the same recipe's two halves, weeks apart.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Tastes like cabbage soupYoung kimchiElder jar; the vinegar patch, honestly labeled
Broth one-note hotGochugaru over-runSix grams holds; more kimchi juice instead
Pork toughBoiled before renderingRender first, always
Tofu crumbledBoiled hard at the endGentle bubble, slabs in last

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 2 days and genuinely improves; day-two jjigae over fresh rice is the dish's own finest hour. (The dolsot's components (#4) and this pot share a fridge rotation.)
  • Variations: the tuna pot (the honest bachelor classic); the ramen drop; spam's island fork; the brothier soup version with more stock and no reduction for the summer table.
